titre: The Act of Settlement Protects Judges, Thirteen Years Later
accroche: In 1701, the English Parliament forbids the king from dismissing judges at will. The measure will take effect only thirteen years later.
contenu_vulgarise:
November 1616, London. Edward Coke, Chief Justice of the King's Bench, refuses a request from King James I: to stay the hearing of a case, the Commendams Case, so that the sovereign can first confer with the judges handling it. Coke stands firm, in the name of a principle he has defended for years: the common law is interpreted by lawyers, not by the royal will. James I rules otherwise and dismisses him from office on November 14, 1616, for no reason other than his insubordination.

## A Judge in Office for as Long as the King Pleases

Nothing, at the time, protects Coke from such a decision. The commissions of English judges are then issued *durante bene placito*, during the king's pleasure. A judge who displeases the Crown can be removed overnight, with no procedure or recourse. The case is not isolated: in 1630, Charles I pushes Sir John Walter, chief baron of the Exchequer, into resigning after he refused to follow the king on a treason prosecution of members of Parliament. Walter nonetheless held a commission drafted *quamdiu se bene gesserint* (for as long as he behaves well), granted by royal grace without the law obliging the sovereign to do so. The proof is made: a practice of goodwill protects no one if the king can simply ask for a resignation.

## A Law That Settles the Matter, Belatedly

The Act of Settlement, passed in 1701 to settle the succession to the throne after the expected death of William III and Anne without a direct heir, seizes the opportunity to rule on judges as well. The text provides that their commissions will henceforth be made *quamdiu se bene gesserint*, their salaries fixed by Parliament, and that they may be removed only upon an address of both Houses. Removal at will ceases to be a royal prerogative: it becomes a parliamentary decision, reasoned and public.

The text, however, does not apply right away. Like all the clauses of the 1701 Act, this one was to take effect only upon the death of William III and Anne, the two sovereigns then living whom the law was precisely meant not to bind. William III dies as early as 1702; Anne reigns until 1714. The guarantee voted in 1701 to protect judges from royal arbitrariness thus becomes effective, in practice, only on August 1, 1714, thirteen years after its adoption, on the day a queen dies whom the text was never meant to concern.

The delay is no mere anecdote. It shows that a guarantee of judicial independence can be passed without any judge benefiting from it for more than a decade. Its force does not come from the date on which Parliament signs it. It comes from the date on which it ceases to be a mere promise made to sovereigns who are no more.

citation.texte: Judges Commissions be made Quam diu se bene Gesserint and their Salaries ascertained and established but upon the Address of both Houses of Parliament it may be lawfull to remove them.
citation.source: Act of Settlement, 12 & 13 Will. III, c. 2, 1701

carte.punch: A 1701 law protects the king's judges, but only from 1714.
carte.idee: In 1701, the English Parliament decides that judges may no longer be dismissed at the king's will, but only upon a joint address of both Houses. The clause was to take effect only on the death of the sovereigns then living: it protected no judge before 1714, thirteen years after its passage.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Cornell's Legal Information Institute traces how the drafters of the U.S. Constitution took up the English formula for Article III.

quiz.question: Why does the guarantee of judicial independence passed by the Act of Settlement in 1701 protect no judge before 1714?
choix: Because Parliament took thirteen years to draft the implementing text of the law
Because it was to take effect only on the death of William III and Anne, who were then alive
Because judges appointed before 1701 first had to take a new oath
Because the House of Lords blocked the text until 1714
quiz.explication: The Act of Settlement settled the succession after William III and Anne, without wanting to bind the sovereigns then reigning: the clause on judges therefore had to wait for both of them to die. William III dies as early as 1702, but Anne reigns until August 1, 1714, the date on which the guarantee finally takes effect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is Edward Coke dismissed from office in 1616?
choix: Because he had issued a judgment unfavorable to the Crown's financial interests
Because he refused to stay the hearing of the Commendams Case at the king's request
Because he had publicly challenged the legitimacy of King James I
Because he refused to recognize Parliament's authority over the courts
quiz_supplementaire.explication: James I wanted to confer with the judges before they ruled on the Commendams Case. Coke refuses to stay the hearing, in the name of the principle that the common law is interpreted by lawyers, and loses his office on November 14, 1616.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the removal of Sir John Walter by Charles I in 1630 reveal?
choix: That a *quamdiu se bene gesserint* commission did not prevent the king from obtaining a resignation
That the judges of the Exchequer were safe from any pressure from the king
That Charles I had to obtain Parliament's consent to dismiss a judge
That Walter had chosen to leave his post himself, with no pressure at all
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Walter nonetheless held a commission drafted *quamdiu se bene gesserint*, a formula granted by royal grace without legal obligation. The precedent shows that such a practice of goodwill protects no judge the king wants to remove.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides the way judges are appointed, what does the Act of Settlement of 1701 change?
choix: Judges are now elected by the two Houses of Parliament
The king keeps his right to remove a judge, but must give public reasons
Their salaries are fixed by Parliament, and their removal requires an address of both Houses
Judges are subject to a seven-year term, renewable once
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text adds two guarantees to *quamdiu se bene gesserint* commissions: salaries voted by Parliament, and removal possible only upon a joint address of both Houses, no longer a decision of the king alone.
